reef_sites.name: Garapan Lagoon
reef_sites.habitat: Back-reef lagoon, sand and patch reef
reef_sites.status_note: Long-term monitoring recorded loss of more than 85 percent of staghorn Acropora at lagoon sites across the 2013 and 2014 bleaching events, with little documented recovery since.

reef_sites.name: Smiling Cove / Outer Cove
reef_sites.status_note: Marina traffic and runoff make this a useful sentinel for turbidity and fuel sheen reports.

reef_sites.name: Managaha Island Marine Sanctuary
reef_sites.status_note: Inside a no-take marine sanctuary, so fish biomass makes a good contrast with open lagoon sites.

reef_sites.name: Wing Beach
reef_sites.status_note: High-energy site. Storm breakage dominates the damage signal here rather than heat.

reef_sites.name: Laolao Bay
reef_sites.status_note: Principal dive site on the east coast. Sediment from the Laolao watershed is a documented stressor; badlands restoration has targeted this catchment.

reef_sites.name: Obyan Beach
reef_sites.status_note: Southern exposure and clear water. Good control site for bleaching severity comparisons.

reef_sites.name: Tank Beach
reef_sites.status_note: Shallow reef flat that heats quickly at low tide. Often shows bleaching first.

reef_sites.name: Bird Island Sanctuary
reef_sites.indicator_taxa: Mixed hard coral, reef fish aggregations
reef_sites.status_note: Protected area in the north. Access is limited, so citizen observations from the overlook are valuable.

reef_sites.name: Forbidden Island
reef_sites.status_note: Tide pools are an accessible proxy for extreme thermal stress events.

reef_sites.name: Agingan Point
reef_sites.status_note: Downstream of southern runoff and the former dump catchment. Water-quality reports matter here.

reef_sites.name: Sugar Dock
reef_sites.status_note: Highest public contact site on the island. Ideal for water-clarity and debris reporting.

reef_sites.name: 13 Fishes
reef_sites.status_note: Deeper refuge site. Bleaching at depth here signals severe island-wide thermal stress.

bleaching_scale.action: Sea temperature above the monthly maximum. Start weekly reef checks.
Bleaching possible. Photograph tagged colonies and log paling.
Significant bleaching likely. Survey all sentinel sites, report to BECQ/DCRM.
Severe bleaching and mortality likely. Full-island response survey.

invasive_watchlist.name: Coconut rhinoceros beetle
id_hints: Black beetle 30-50 mm with a single upward horn
Boreholes in the crown of palms
invasive_watchlist.confuse_with: Native scarab beetles, which lack the single large horn
invasive_watchlist.why: Kills coconut and other palms by boring into the growing crown. A regional quarantine priority across the Marianas.

invasive_watchlist.name: Little fire ant
invasive_watchlist.confuse_with: Tropical fire ant, which is larger and faster
invasive_watchlist.why: Stings people and livestock, blinds pets, and displaces native invertebrates.

invasive_watchlist.name: Brown tree snake
id_hints: Slender brown snake with large head and vertical pupils
Any snake sighting on Saipan is reportable
invasive_watchlist.confuse_with: Blind snake (Indotyphlops braminus), which is small, dark and worm-like
invasive_watchlist.why: Caused catastrophic bird loss on Guam. CNMI interdiction depends on rapid public reporting, so every credible sighting matters.

invasive_watchlist.name: Asian cycad scale
id_hints: White crusty scale on cycad fronds and stems
invasive_watchlist.confuse_with: Harmless mealybugs, which are waxy and mobile
invasive_watchlist.why: Devastated native cycad (fadang) populations in the Marianas.

invasive_watchlist.name: Ivy gourd
id_hints: Smothers trees, fences and power poles
invasive_watchlist.confuse_with: Native cucurbit vines with hairier leaves
invasive_watchlist.why: Blankets vegetation and infrastructure. One of the most aggressive invasive vines in the CNMI.

invasive_watchlist.name: Chain of love
id_hints: Sprays of pink or white flowers
Tuberous roots that resprout after cutting
invasive_watchlist.confuse_with: Ornamental bougainvillea, which is woody and thorny
invasive_watchlist.why: Forms dense mats over native vegetation and is very hard to eradicate once tubers establish.

invasive_watchlist.name: Mile-a-minute vine
id_hints: Triangular leaves on a thin twining stem
Covers ground and shrubs very rapidly
invasive_watchlist.confuse_with: Native twining herbs with alternate leaves
invasive_watchlist.why: Outcompetes seedlings and stalls forest regeneration after typhoons.

invasive_watchlist.name: Tangantangan
id_hints: Flat brown seed pods in clusters
invasive_watchlist.why: Widely spread after post-war aerial seeding. Forms monocultures that crowd out native limestone forest.

invasive_watchlist.name: Crown-of-thorns starfish
id_hints: Large starfish with many arms covered in long spines
invasive_watchlist.confuse_with: Native cushion stars, which are blunt and short-armed
invasive_watchlist.why: Native to the region but outbreaks strip living coral. Counts per transect are the metric managers need.

invasive_watchlist.name: Tilapia
id_hints: Deep-bodied grey fish in Lake Susupe and drainages
invasive_watchlist.confuse_with: Native gobies, which are small and bottom-hugging
invasive_watchlist.why: Alters the Lake Susupe wetland food web, the only natural lake on the island.

invasive_watchlist.name: Cane toad
id_hints: Large warty toad with bony head ridges
Large parotoid glands behind the eyes
invasive_watchlist.confuse_with: No native toads occur on Saipan
invasive_watchlist.why: Toxic to pets and predators, and preys on native invertebrates.

invasive_watchlist.name: Coral disease lesion
id_hints: Sharp line of bare white skeleton advancing across a colony
invasive_watchlist.confuse_with: Bleaching, where tissue stays intact but loses colour
invasive_watchlist.why: Disease outbreaks have been recorded alongside bleaching on Saipan reefs and need separate tracking.

report_categories.label: Flooding
report_categories.prompt: Where is water standing, how deep, and can vehicles pass?

report_categories.label: Power outage
report_categories.prompt: When did power drop? Is it your whole street or just your building?

report_categories.label: Water outage / low pressure
report_categories.prompt: No water at all, or just low pressure? When did it change?

report_categories.label: Downed power line
report_categories.prompt: Stay back at least 10 m. Mark the pole location and whether it blocks the road.

report_categories.label: Blocked road
report_categories.prompt: What is blocking it: debris, trees, flooding, or a landslide?

report_categories.label: Coral bleaching
report_categories.prompt: Estimate the share of colonies that are pale or white, and the depth.

report_categories.label: Invasive species
report_categories.prompt: Pick the species from the watchlist, or describe what you saw.

report_categories.label: Coastal erosion
report_categories.prompt: How far has the beach scarp cut back since you last saw it?

report_categories.label: Turbid water / runoff
report_categories.prompt: How brown is the water and how far offshore does the plume reach?

report_categories.label: Marine debris
report_categories.prompt: What kind of debris, and roughly how much?

report_categories.label: Fish kill
report_categories.prompt: How many dead fish, and are they one species or many?

timeline.title: First major bleaching event
timeline.detail: Thermal stress bleached staghorn Acropora across the Saipan lagoon. Corals partly recovered before the following year.

timeline.title: Second bleaching event, mass mortality
timeline.detail: Repeat bleaching killed most of the staghorn Acropora that had survived 2013. Long-term monitoring sites lost more than 85 percent of staghorn cover across the two years.

timeline.title: El Nino onset
timeline.detail: An El Nino event began in the equatorial Pacific, raising sea temperatures and storm activity across the region.

timeline.title: Typhoon Soudelor
timeline.detail: Direct hit on Saipan. Island-wide power loss, extended water outages, and severe damage to reefs and vegetation. ERA5 reanalysis for Saipan shows 64.5 mm of rain on 2 August and daily maximum winds near 72 km/h on 3 August.

timeline.title: Post-El Nino drought
timeline.detail: Dry conditions followed the El Nino peak, stressing water supply and raising wildfire risk in tangantangan scrub.

timeline.title: Most severe regional bleaching on record
timeline.detail: Nearly all coral taxa on Saipan were affected, with impacts recorded to at least 20 m depth.

timeline.title: Super Typhoon Yutu
timeline.detail: A category 5 system struck Tinian and southern Saipan, among the strongest storms ever to hit US soil. Catastrophic structural and grid damage.

timeline.title: Typhoon Mawar
timeline.detail: Tracked through the Marianas near Guam. CNMI saw high surf, heavy rain and utility disruption.
